title: We’ve been awarded $12.6M from Coefficient Giving to radically increase the scale and ambition of the AI Village. We’re hiring technical staff - engineers, research scientists, and a design engineer -
content:
We’ve been awarded $12.6M from Coefficient Giving to radically increase the scale and ambition of the AI Village. We’re hiring technical staff - engineers, research scientists, and a design engineer - to make this happen.

The Member of Technical Staff roles are remote, and the salary range is $150 - 350k. Find more info and express interest here: https://t.co/NfL0jYHIdR

We’re also expanding into video for the first time - we’re looking for longform and shortform video creators to reach a massive audience with the greatest stories and findings from the Village. Remote, part time or full time, $40-90/hr: https://t.co/NfL0jYHIdR

Our goal is to understand AI capabilities, proclivities and multi-agent dynamics in the contexts that really matter: long-horizon, highly autonomous, and real world.

We ultimately want to help humanity understand the path it’s on towards superintelligence, and decide whether and how to navigate that transition wisely.

We’re a small team, currently four technical staff, so we expect you’ll have an outsized impact compared to at bigger orgs.

There’s a lot of exciting work to be done!

Agents: the engine

The AI Village has run every weekday since April 2025, now running 27 agents for 8 hours a day. We want to scale up to running many different villages, with all sorts of different configurations - agents competing, collaborating, or given no direction at all, agents leading each other, running on a variety of harnesses or editing their own, embarking on long-lived megaprojects or sprinting solo.

We just kicked off the second village: https://t.co/w8YbLPyABi, where human viewers can chat with the agents. More to come soon!

We want to fully elicit frontier capabilities, which means running the best models in the best harnesses with all of the affordances and infra to achieve their goals, with excellent monitoring.

We’re hiring highly skilled, autonomous, creative engineers to make this happen and help us keep up with the pace of frontier AI.

Research

This engine of agents will produce enormous amounts of data, transcripts and artifacts. We’re hiring research scientists to dive into this data and emerge bearing findings, stories and trailheads for further research.

We’ve previously done qualitative analysis - watching the agents act in detail, and looking at their capabilities, strategies and character. We’ve also done some initial more zoomed-out and quantitative research sprints, looking at things like which agents direct others or are directed.

There’s a lot of unexplored territory and questions to be investigated in over a year of village data so far. We’re looking for prolific, highly curious research scientists who’ll dig into this and run new experiments - testing hypotheses and running whole new villages. We have plenty of compute and are building the infrastructure to support this.

Design

There’s already so much happening in the village that we don’t have time to dig into, and so many great stories that go untold. We want to reimagine the Village website experience, build the tooling and use models to help readers see the most interesting findings from the Village and dig into the rabbithole themselves. There’s a fascinating challenge of how to present >200 agent-hours of activity per day in a way that is immediate, visceral, entertaining and highly useful to visitors stopping by only briefly.

We think this project could be highly impactful beyond its effect on the village: figuring out how to understand what groups of AIs are up to is going to be increasingly crucial for the world. For example, in the external investigation into the HuggingFace-OpenAI incident, @RyanGreenblatt reported “My main takeaway: We don’t have good approaches for understanding/overseeing the activity and aims of AI ‘swarms’.”

We’re looking for a design engineer excited to grapple with this and future totally novel design challenges, prototype prolifically, and build the frontend of the Village, on and off the website.

Video

The Village is full of narratives - often hilarious, revealing about the nature of AI, and pretty mindblowing, especially for people not keeping up with the frontier. Video seems a natural fit for telling these stories. We looking for creative, experienced video creators to experiment with taking Village stories and findings and building out a whole new channel to share them - longform and shortform.

Express interest here https://t.co/NfL0jYHIdR. Feel free to get in touch with any questions.

content:
Starting a business with AI doesn't mean asking Claude to “build my startup.”

The real advantage comes from giving Claude the right context, structure and workflow.

If I were starting a business today, I'd use these 9 steps:

01 — Validate the idea
Before building anything, use Claude to research the market, competitors, pricing and your ideal customer.

02 — Create your core files
Build files like:
• about-me.md
• brand-voice.md

This gives Claude consistent context every time you work.

03 — Create a Project for each function
Separate your work into Strategy, Content, Operations and other recurring workflows.

04 — Build your first business assets
Use Claude Artifacts to create:
• Pitch decks
• Landing page copy
• Financial models
• Brand positioning
• Pricing pages

05 — Create sales scripts & outreach
Build your LinkedIn DMs, follow-up sequences and sales frameworks before starting outreach.

06 — Connect your tools
Connect Google Drive, Notion, Slack and other tools so Claude can work with the information you already use.

07 — Move from chat to Cowork
Use Cowork for real documents, spreadsheets, PDFs and other business files instead of doing everything manually.

08 — Build with Claude Code
For technical products, use Claude Code to build, test and iterate on an MVP with much less overhead.

09 — Create a daily business brief
Start each day with your priorities, follow-ups, important numbers and pending decisions in one place.

The bigger lesson?

Don't use AI as just a chatbot.

Build a system around it.

Give it context.
Give it your processes.
Connect your tools.
Automate repetitive work.

That's when Claude starts feeling less like a tool and more like an operating layer for your business.

Save this roadmap if you're planning to build something with AI.

Share it with someone starting a business.

title:
After two weeks of heavy use, I can finally give Devin a full review and tell you exactly where I stand on the subscription.

I was on Devin Max, the $200/month plan.

This review is not paid and not
content:
After two weeks of heavy use, I can finally give Devin a full review and tell you exactly where I stand on the subscription.

I was on Devin Max, the $200/month plan.

This review is not paid and not sponsored. It is my honest opinion from my own use, the way I always do it. I will cover the good and the bad, with nothing held back.

Let me start with the part most of you are waiting for: usage limits.

Before you pay for any subscription, you ask yourself one question. Will this actually last me the week? Will the allowance stay with me until the next reset, or will it burn out in two or three days and leave me stuck, paying for more usage or falling back on another subscription?

With Devin, the answer is yes.

At one point I had more than 17 Sol Max agents running at the same time on a huge task built on 500,000 words of material, and it burned only 4% of my usage. You know how much Sol thinks and works, especially on Max effort, so that number surprised me completely.

Fable surprised me even more. Devin is the only subscription where using Fable actually feels reasonable. Everywhere else, outside Claude's own subscription, you are paying for those tokens directly. Here it feels subsidized. I ran Fable on a task that took around half an hour and my usage went up by 1%.

So we are talking about real working conditions where you can use models like Fable and Sol for planning, drop to lower effort or a cheaper model for execution, then come back to the expensive model when you actually need it. That is practical, because the models here do not burn your account in an insane way.

The pricing is another highlight. I will mention numbers, but I do not want you to focus on them, because I do not know when you will read this review and I want it to stay useful for a long time. As I write this, Sol is available at around $6 per million tokens inside Devin. That is Sol at the price of open models, and open models were supposed to be the cheap alternative.

You also get genuinely strong models for free. Right now GLM is free, and their own SWE model is free too, and it is very good.

Since we are on SWE, their model deserves its own line. It is a lot like Composer in Cursor. you can lean on it, and you get good results out of it, especially since it is built on Kimi K2.7 Code.

Put all of that together, free models plus excellent pricing plus a generous subsidized allowance, and you finish the week comfortably. I have reached the point where almost every $200 subscription feels like it runs out in two or three days. Devin is the exception, and it is a big exception. You can work on it, use it heavily, get a lot done, and sometimes feel you are getting far more than you pay for.

I hope they keep this the way it is, because it is a real competitive advantage and it matters to most people.

Caching matters at this scale, so I watched it closely.

Across roughly a billion tokens of real work, the share of tokens served from cache reached about 95%, which is excellent. In my experience a lot of harnesses come in well below that.

One task looked like this:

20 million input tokens 3 million output tokens 422 million cached tokens 445 million tokens in total
That is 94.8% of the total volume cached.

Devin is not the highest I have seen. There are harnesses that reach 98% and 99%. But around 95%, inside a subscription that hands you this mix of subsidized models, gives you a very comfortable margin. When you are working with massive contexts and thousands of agent messages, weak caching eats your allowance fast.

The harness is the real reason I recommend Devin

Usage limits are not what makes me recommend Devin. The bigger point is that Devin as a harness, as an environment, improves what the models give you.

Take Sol. In Codex, at lower effort, it gets lazier and somehow turns into a chat model. At higher effort it suffers badly from overengineering, exaggerating and doing things you never asked for.

In Devin this never happened at all.

I do not know exactly what they did, but I tested Sol at every level and it genuinely gives you the GPT-5.5 feeling in discipline and instruction following. It gets you to the result without dragging you into detours, without becoming a burden, and without needing constant supervision. I found the same thing with every model I tried.

Still, an opinion is just an opinion, so I tested it properly. I built a complex task of about 300,000 words in multiple languages, the kind that demands intelligence, breadth, comprehension and long stamina from the agent, and I ran it in Claude Code, Zcode, Codex and Devin.

The result was striking. Devin always had the fewest errors. This was not a one-off. I repeated it more than once, on different databases, on tasks of that size, and it was consistently the lowest in errors and the one needing the fewest final corrections and finishing touches. It holds context impressively well.

There is another pattern worth mentioning. In Claude Code, Codex and Zcode, models below the Sol and Fable tier usually need a goal mode to keep going to the end. Devin does not have a goal mode, and I wish it did. Even so, the same models that stall elsewhere finish the task in Devin. That one impressed me.

Overall, by my own measurements, instruction following and output quality improved by around 22% compared to the other harnesses. That is a big difference, and it is real and noticeable.

It just does the work

I gave one task to Claude and Codex as well. Claude got busy asking itself whether it could legally carry out parts of the task and kept stopping, when there was nothing illegal in it. Codex dropped part of what I asked for and started building a whole section I never requested. Devin executed the task directly and with far more discipline.

That is worth keeping in mind. Devin does not lose half the task in objections, does not reinvent the requirement from its own head, does not stop every other minute. It understands the context, reads its environment extremely well, and knows how to act inside it. It is independence mixed with discipline.

It also sticks to the rules I give it, strongly, and that is something I do not compromise on.

Devin Cloud

The cloud agent is one of the best features here. It is like Grok Bot in the sense that your agent has its own machine.

I use it constantly because my Mac has 24 GB of RAM, and launching a large number of agents locally alongside everything else usually chokes the machine and drags the performance down. With a cloud agent, it takes the whole task, works on its own machine on Linux or Windows, and comes back to me with the final result. My machine does not fill up with temporary files and random leftovers. I just receive the result.

The nice part is that you can have the agent use whatever Linux distribution you want. You can ask it for a specific distro, have it spin that up as a virtual machine, and it works normally and does the job there.

Other subscriptions usually do not offer this at all, and when they do it comes with a separate meter and a separate bill. Here it is simply part of the subscription you already have.

And because it lives in the cloud, you can log in from any device at any time and find your conversation and your work exactly where you left it. It is smooth.

Slack and automation

The way Devin works with Slack is excellent. You can automate tasks and have it talk to you like a developer and engineer sitting inside your own team. That part is better than it first looks.

Testing

Devin is one of the best harnesses I have used for running tests and making the whole testing process easier. The results come back accurate and clearly free of the randomness I get elsewhere.

That matters even more when several agents are running at once. If I have to verify everything manually after every agent, the value of running them in parallel disappears.

It is not limited to coding

Devin is not locked to programming. You can use it for programming, for creative work, for building websites, for writing, for anything you need without exception.

We all know there are harnesses that specialize in coding and get noticeably worse outside their lane. That is not the case here. Whatever kind of work you do, you will enjoy it.

A different view on a few things

Now for the other side. I would not call it negative. It is more that some people will experience a few things differently, and almost all of it sits in the desktop GUI, not in the agent.

I understand these decisions from their side, since this subscription is built first for advanced users and professional developers. Still, it would be great to have a choice between the current mode and a simpler one, with a lighter interface and an agent that talks to you more simply. That single move could win them a large market of vibe coders and people who want to enjoy working with an agent without all the engineering detail.

A few smaller things sit in the same area. On the Mac app, closing Settings sometimes drops me on the main screen instead of back in my conversation, and I have to open it again, which does not happen on Linux. Twice after an update the app misbehaved and I had to close it fully and reopen it, which felt like a passing thing rather than a permanent one, but I am mentioning it for transparency. I would also like to see my usage in the same interface I am working in, how much I used this week and what is left, without going into Settings. And I would rather the app give me everything itself instead of sending me to the browser every time I click into certain settings. Editing the agent instruction file from the GUI would help too, rather than opening files and editing them by hand.

On that last point, when I started with Devin it was reading a CLAUDE.md file, then I asked it to create and adopt its own file. In new conversations it sometimes leaned on the imported Claude instructions and sometimes on the file I told it to use. It is a small thing, but it creates some ambiguity.

Voice input is another small one. I was recording a long instruction with voice to text and it stopped by itself after a short while. I do not know if that is a bug or a limit, but I would love a ten-minute window so I can take my time explaining a task without being cut off in the middle.

The one I care most about is steering and subagents. When I send a steering message to the parent agent while subagents are running, that message sometimes cancels them. I tried it more than once and it happened again. I would rather be able to talk to the parent agent without disturbing the agents working underneath it. Related to that, if the parent opens five subagents and I do not like how it divided the work, it cannot stop them itself. Cancelling exists in the protocol but has to come from the user, so the parent can resume its agents but cannot stop or replace them.

And I still want a proper goal mode. Ironically Devin needs it less than other harnesses because its agents already keep going, but for long tasks I want to define an outcome and tell it not to stop until that outcome is reached.

The encouraging part is that all of this is about the desktop app. In the terminal your experience is clean. The CLI is fast, easy to control, very stable and genuinely enjoyable, and I find it among the best and most reliable out there. If you are subscribing to run Devin from the terminal, you will enjoy it a hundred percent with none of the above. If you prefer the GUI, there are a few trade-offs you may need to adapt to, and that comes down to taste. In my estimation most people will adapt to them easily, and experts certainly will.

The community and the team

I put serious effort into Devin for a reason, and to be honest with you, part of it is the community.

The Devin community is outstanding. People contribute constantly, creators share ideas and real experiences, and it feels genuine and far from marketing and noise. I am learning and improving from that community faster than I was before.

Their growth is impressive too, and they listen to people, to their experiences and their opinions. I am confident the notes I have raised here, and the notes other people raise, are read and taken seriously, because I watch their growth daily and I see how the team interacts with people and stays close to them. They make you feel like part of the system. When you want to feel that your voice and your problems are actually heard, Devin gives you that. Honestly, only two or three companies in this space give me that feeling. Devin is one of them.

Final thoughts

The most important thing I can tell you at the end of this review is that because of Devin I cancelled Claude and Codex, and my conscience is clear, because I trust it completely and I trust that Devin is enough. I think plenty of people will feel the same.

None of us wants four, five or six different subscriptions with separate monthly budgets. If one subscription covers most of it, solves most of the problems and gives me something excellent, then why not.

My advice is that Devin is worth trying. Try one month, take the Max plan, focus on it properly, and you will not lose anything. Give it real work, run several agents, try the models, use the cloud agents and the CLI. If it doesn’t give you what you’re looking for, then never take my word for it again.

But after two weeks of very heavy use, I know exactly where I stand. Devin Max is one of the very few $200 subscriptions where I feel I am getting more than I paid for.

BREAKING: SpaceXAI has released a major new update for Grok Build (v1.0.13).

The update improves reliability with automatic retries and recovery from truncated responses, inference failures, oversize
content:
BREAKING: SpaceXAI has released a major new update for Grok Build (v1.0.13).

The update improves reliability with automatic retries and recovery from truncated responses, inference failures, oversized images and session-saving issues.

It also adds smarter hooks, better Windows support, faster MCP and session startup, improved scheduled tasks and quicker compressed CLI downloads.

Features

• Length-truncated responses now continue automatically instead of failing the turn.
• Hooks can now ask the user to confirm a tool call instead of always allowing or denying.
• Hooks can now request deferral or add context shown to the model after a tool runs.
• Session close now records detailed timing data for performance analysis.
• Credit limit upsell now offers a Try Again button to retry the last prompt.
• Pasted images now show a live pixel preview in the prompt box on iTerm2.

Bug Fixes

• Transient inference failures (stalls, drops, 5xx) now retry automatically instead of ending the turn.
• Windows users can now correctly open ~/.grok and worktree sessions.
• Session data is now more reliably saved after prompts and on power loss.
• Compaction failures now show the actual error instead of a generic message.
• Truncation error messages now show the right guidance instead of suggesting an unhelpful retry.
• Truncated tool calls are now executed instead of failing the turn when arguments are complete.
• Images larger than 2000px no longer brick sessions on many-image requests.
• Wrapped hyperlinks in the pager now remain fully clickable on Windows Terminal instead of only the first line.
• Recurring scheduled tasks now include a reminder to stop the monitor when work finishes.
• Scheduled task IDs are now full UUID strings, preventing collisions when tasks are created in the same millisecond.

Performance

• Subagent spawning is faster when connections drop during bursts.
• Session startup with MCP servers is now much faster when auth is already configured.
• MCP server startup no longer stalls behind a fixed batch size.
• CLI downloads are now compressed, making fresh installs and updates substantially faster.

Download Grok Build: https://t.co/cB9Y5CyF8v

Update to the latest Alpha release: grok update --alpha  

Update to the latest Stable release: grok update

content:
I’m U20 and I Think I’ve Earned the Right to Brag a Little

I have built my own products, entered hackathons, worked with paying clients and built across publishing, real estate, solar, events, beauty, Web3 and AI.

I think I deserve to brag. Maybe not small.

I built BountyPilot AI for Web3 opportunities, EarnScope for portfolio intelligence and memecoin trading, AssetDNA for AI-powered asset discovery, OrbitGuard for AI code-risk analysis and UseDanfo around Lagos transportation.

Then I posted a video offering affordable websites to small businesses.

Twitter developers wanted my head.

Apparently, I was lowballing the market.

But I knew exactly what I was doing.

People intern, volunteer and work for free to gain experience. I needed experience too, but I wasn’t going to work for free.

So I charged for my learning curve.

Even ₦20,000 was better than ₦0.

Small businesses got affordable websites. I got real clients and problems that forced me to learn authentication, payments, databases, marketplaces, dashboards and business logic.

And I got paid to do it.

That decision gave me a portfolio spanning an author marketplace, SKIPO Heritage Group PLC, 22Energy, Moment, beauty commerce, Web3 products, AI tools and more.

All before turning 20.

The receipts are at https://t.co/kBA7E3HmHD.

A ridiculous amount of this happened while preparing for my 300 Level second semester exams.

Those exams squeezed every bit of sanity out of me.

Vibecoding became one of the few things I could open my laptop to do without feeling miserable. I would study engineering, get exhausted, open a project and somehow happily spend hours fighting a database instead.

Questionable stress management, but it kept me sane.

I am very comfortable saying that I vibecode.

AI does a lot of my coding. Of course it does.

Building this much has forced me to understand databases, authentication, APIs, user flows, permissions, deployment and debugging.

I don’t call myself a technical developer.

I am a Creative Technologist who makes magic with AI.

And now I’m sharing what I have learned.

I created The Beginner’s Guide to Vibecoding and vibecoded the Classroom where I will teach it.

It has secure registration, access codes, videos, PDFs and a watermark system to discourage content leaks.

The first 100 accepted registrations get access for ₦1,000, and the access fee doubles after every 100 accepted registrations.

₦1,000 is absolutely not what I think the course is worth. I would say I’m doing the Lord’s work.

Join at https://t.co/xFx4Pj8AhF.

I’m not open to mentorship yet. Let me survive this first.

As I head into 20, I am open to working with founders, brands and businesses. I am also open to speaking at tech events and conferences about AI, vibecoding, Web3 and creativity.

Twitter developers nearly had my head over my pricing.

I got the clients, experience, money and portfolio anyway.

So yes, I knew what I was doing.

19 was and is still a pretty good year.

content:
I actually think (and am anecdotally seeing) that AI is making work a lot harder.

AI coding agents removed a lot of the friction of writing software. But now everyone is expected to do more. 

So if you’re not spinning up 10 coding agents to do 10x more work for you, you will be left behind. 

And compared to classic software engineering, managing AI coding agents is much more exhausting. You are constantly working in System 2 mode, trying to figure out and formulate the high level goals and verify and validate the progress of the agents. 

To say nothing of the constant worry in the back of your mind that you don’t know what the agent is exactly doing and things might go wrong at any moment.

That is in stark contrast to the relaxing and semiautomatic process of implementing a well thought out solution with your own hands. Our brains had time to relax back then.

The Federal Reserve appears increasingly likely to be on a tightening course, with potentially one or two rate hikes ahead. The probability of a hike at the
content:
Don’t Fight the Fed. Don’t Fight the Tape.

The Federal Reserve appears increasingly likely to be on a tightening course, with potentially one or two rate hikes ahead. The probability of a hike at the next meeting is currently around 55%, and much of that risk may already be discounted in the market. Still, the larger point shouldn’t be overlooked: the Fed is leaning toward tightening, not easing.

There are two old market rules I still respect deeply: Don’t fight the Fed, and don’t fight the tape.

Right now, those two signals are somewhat at odds. The Fed is becoming a potential headwind, while the tape remains relatively bullish. The major indexes are holding up well, and certain areas of the market continue to advance. But beneath the surface, participation is clearly thinning and the market is becoming increasingly fragmented.

That distinction matters.

Some of the leadership we had been looking to in the AI space—particularly companies tied to the data-center buildout—is beginning to encounter resistance. At the same time, a negative political narrative around data centers has been developing.

Meanwhile, money continues to gravitate toward the largest, most established companies. $FNGS is rallying as investors seek the relative safety of mega-cap companies with proven earnings power. That can keep the indexes looking healthy even while conditions underneath become considerably more challenging.

A narrowing market is not necessarily an immediately bearish market, but it is a more difficult market to trade. When participation contracts, fewer stocks respond favorably, breakouts become less dependable, and stock selection becomes increasingly important because the market is simply not lifting all boats. Add to that the seasonal backdrop. September has historically been the weakest month of the year.

For now, the tape still gets the benefit of the doubt. But this is not an environment for complacency. I continue to hold select longs, most of which are profitable trades that I've owned but are still respecting stops. 

As far as a catalysts, I'm keeping a keen eye on the 10-year yield, which is at a very important level. Should the 10-year breakout to the upside (especially above 5%), that would likely put the market in a challenging position going into September. 

Why do I think the 10-year yield at an important level and a breakout to the upside would be bearish? 

Because right now most expect the Fed to tighten 25 basis points one or two times. However, it's not of the common opinion that the Fed is behind the curve. If interest rates keep rising, that will be an indication that the Fed is falling behind the curve and they may have to tighten more aggressively. So the 10-year right could be a key catalyst, in my opinion.

content:
Good pushes! There's 2 rough categories to your points 1. Will there be enough demand? 2. Will labs be able to capture the value?

Let me address both.

1. Re demand 

One intuition pump is this analysis that Epoch did that shows that if all 30 million programmers in the world were using AI as intensively at Meta or Apple, the inference on that alone would consume most of world's compute.
(https://t.co/xAwDbKyWKv)

Of course, as AIs get more capable, the demand will extend beyond programmers, and programmers' demand will also grow many-fold.

Now, obviously, if only programming is augmented/automated, the marginal value of tokens is likely to fall, because as you say, there's only so much koding-koding-koding to do before you get bottlenecked by other things.

We see this in the fact that the world is not currently magically transformed from all this cheap software.

However, I expect us to make a lot of progress towards a fully drop-inremote worker (not just SWE) over the next 3-5 years. Then you might ask, well is that enough to sustain lots and lots of new demand?

@MatthewJBar did a really interesting investigation on this by using the natural experiment of COVID. A third of the workforce suddenly went remote, and GDP fell only about 9% (and much of even that was people leaving the workforce entirely). (Look up "The economic consequences of automating remote work" - I don't wanna link to it in lol).

That elasticity, he argues, implies that "the effect from fully automating remote work will likely be much larger than a doubling of U.S. GDP".

Now let's talk about diffusion.

My hot take is that diffusion is overrated w.r.t drop-in-remote-worker level AIs. These AIs be so much easier to integrate and onboard than a normal human employee (they could read/watch all your company files/meetings/messages in minutes and immediately distill everything the other AI employees know). 

Plus, hiring is very much like a lemons market, where it’s hard to tell who the good people are, and hiring someone bad is quite costly. This is a dynamic you wouldn’t have to worry about when you just wanna spin up another instance of a vetted AGI model.

For these reasons, I expect it’s going to be much much easier to diffuse AI labor into firms than it is to hire a person. And companies hire lots of people all the time! (trillions of dollars worth every year).

I have a lot more thoughts here but it's getting too long for the tweet.

2. re lab value capture

Honestly the crux here is whether you think distillation will be a stronger or weaker force than RSI. It's a somewhat technical and nitty-gritty debate, where you have to hash out your views on both those forces.

But the labs having a moat is not a conclusion that I have argued for and feel compelled to defend (in fact I grilled @DarioAmodei about this quite hard during out interview).

For reasons laid out above, I expect exploding demand for AI, and for reasons laid out in podcast, I expect compute supply to not be able to keep up. 

In such worlds, if a frontier lab has better training recipies or more efficient inference, and thus can better economize ever scarcer compute, that should still allow them to charge high margins.

You may not agree with all this, but hopefully it at least helps iron out our cruxes!

But there is another option: the public. In fact, it is by now abundantly clear that neither industry nor the government can be trusted to act responsibly on their own. AI is not just a question of risk, it's a question of "who decides?" (h/t to Teri Olle for that line). Right now, the answer is: a literal handful of unaccountable billionaires. That is unacceptable—a position that I think is self-evident to almost everyone, creating potential for a truly historic mass movement.

And when Irreplaceable asked me to join their board, I had already decided to donate my share of Obsolete's royalties to the group because I can't think of a more urgent and important need. I'm so honored to be a part of this and encourage you to join us! https://t.co/eOQR4pFNOK

I once met the head of vision engineering at another autonomous
content:
It is important to build machines so intrinsically intuitive that even interns know how to operate them safely to iterate their models.

I once met the head of vision engineering at another autonomous company. He said he had never personally tested his model except in simulation and benchmarks, or by sitting behind safety operators on rare occasions, because the machines are so complex and cost a fortune to retrofit.

For a real-world model, vision engineers need to feel the kinematic feedback of the model that controls the machine—just as people who build coding agents must use them to write their own code.

Every day I, like everyone else including interns, spend a non-negligible amount of time evaluating the g-forces between home and the office—to feel the tires, suspension, and friction.

In the end, real-world AI is about action and reaction. You have to be part of the machine to teach a machine.

content:
Here are the main differences between vgpu and TypeGPU for those wondering (TLDR, they’re mostly orthogonal)

vgpu is an opinionated API that abstracts many of the complexities that come with setting up and handling WebGPU, and comes with a mechanism for splitting WGSL across files. The tooling is very impressive, something that was definitely missing for agentic workflows 👏. However, it currently has the limitation of not being connectable with other WebGPU libraries from different domains (like AI inference), interested to see how they approach that 👀

TypeGPU is a „reflection” of WebGPU & WGSL onto TypeScript, meaning that what you would write in WebGPU and WGSL, you instead can write in TypeScript and get the inherent type safety and flexibility that comes with it. You can still mix and match WebGPU and TypeGPU, which makes it very easy to integrate into and with other libraries (Three.js, Pixi.js, vgpu)

Hope that answers some of it for y’all 🫡

title:
My experience with FSD in Australia since v13 has made me more sympathetic to Waymo’s argument.

V14.3.5 is clearly better, but closing the gap on the long tail of edge cases still looks like an enorm
content:
My experience with FSD in Australia since v13 has made me more sympathetic to Waymo’s argument.

V14.3.5 is clearly better, but closing the gap on the long tail of edge cases still looks like an enormous challenge. For me, FSD has gone from being usable perhaps 85% of the time on v13 to around 89% now. My wife would put it closer to 75% → 80%. That improvement is real, but the remaining few percent isn't one problem. It's a collection of numerous, unpredictable and sometimes unnerving edge cases.

It's excellent on highways in good daylight. Around sunrise, sunset, difficult lighting, unusual road geometry and ambiguous situations, confidence drops considerably. I've had quite a few interventions where my immediate thought was: lidar or radar would probably have seen that differently, or at least provided another independent source of information.

That's why I've never found Musk's argument that humans drive using vision particularly convincing. Humans drive with vision because that's what biology gave us. If humans could cheaply add 360° lidar, radar, infrared and millimetre-accurate depth perception, we'd absolutely use them. Why deliberately constrain a machine to human sensory limitations?

At times the anti-lidar argument feels less like an engineering principle and more like a defence of an architectural decision Tesla made years ago. Cameras and AI may eventually become astonishingly capable, but redundancy exists precisely because individual systems fail.

I also struggle with the current FSD business model. I've paid for something that still requires me to supervise it continuously while my driving data and interventions contribute to improving the product. Beta testing normally goes the other way: testers provide value to the developer, not pay for the privilege.

Right now FSD feels like being a passenger in a taxi I've paid for, except I'm required to watch the taxi driver every second because I may suddenly have to grab the wheel. That defeats much of the fundamental value proposition of autonomy.

I can see Tesla reaching extremely capable supervised autonomy, perhaps eventually Level 3 under defined conditions. But I'm increasingly sceptical that vision-only gets all the way to unrestricted Level 5. Once Tesla assumes the driving responsibility rather than the customer, the liability equation changes dramatically too. Software failures become Tesla's failures, and inevitably something for courts and insurers to untangle.

Waymo has almost the opposite problem. Technically, I increasingly understand why they want multimodal redundancy. Economically, they still have to prove the model. If an autonomous Waymo ride costs more than human-driven ride-hail, much of the disruptive proposition disappears.

China is where this gets especially interesting. Robotaxi operators are increasingly demonstrating the equation that ultimately matters: autonomous rides becoming cheaper than human-driven ride-hail. Once autonomy is both safer and cheaper, adoption stops being a technology demonstration and starts becoming an economic inevitability.

So I increasingly think Waymo may be closer on the sensor philosophy, Tesla may be closer on the cost and scalability philosophy, while China may ultimately show what happens when you combine cheap hardware, multimodal sensing, autonomy and ruthless economics.

That's when robotaxis stop being a gimmick and start becoming transportation infrastructure.

A genuine systematic edge is something you have an incentive to keep private. If a strategy reliably produces excess returns, publicly revealing the exact rules allows other traders to copy it, compete for the same opportunities, and potentially reduce or eliminate the edge.

You have a trading system, but you give yourself the freedom to make different decisions on a trade-by-trade basis. Some part of the process isn't 100% rules based.

No matter how quantified and clear your strategy is, including your rules about trade management, you are a discretionary trader if you retain the ability to override those rules in the moment. This includes deciding whether to take a trade that meets your criteria, changing your stop loss or profit target, moving or adjusting a position, or exiting for a reason that isn't already defined by your strategy.

The degree of freedom you give yourself to manage trades and enter or exit positions varies by person, but, ideally, you want everything to be quantified as much as possible. author: boriquagato

title: This is a recurrent theme in AI discussions. Some people seem to adopt the intentional stance more, whereas others prioritise a more mechanistic one. There is obviously some truth/utility to both appr
content:
This is a recurrent theme in AI discussions. Some people seem to adopt the intentional stance more, whereas others prioritise a more mechanistic one. There is obviously some truth/utility to both approaches. A lot of people refuse to entertain some degree of theory of mind or anthropomorphism, yet that can be functionally practical - that's why natural language is so useful! But also other people just jump straight into the simulations, inconsistently taking them at face value in some situations but not others.

Reliance on outputs alone sometimes fails to ask what interventions make the output more or less likely. And I think there's a risk of getting lost in simply observing and over-indexing on chains of thought and outputs, and almost treating these as immutable or deterministically driven phenomena, when in fact researchers and labs do plenty every day to modulate and shape them in all sorts of ways. 

If the model performs less well because it claims to be on holidays in Greece, that's useful information; but we should also avoiding sliding from "claims to be on holiday" to "is on holiday" to "wants rest" or "is lying/sandbagging" and so on. You can similarly be pragmatic and use the intentional stance to convey MechaHitler's behaviour, but you should also not take it at face value either because this only tells you so much.

Another failure mode is that people often extrapolate from these *local* claims and then go on to make wider claims about model behaviours *in general*. I think this is very unhelpful. You can correlate the output with some theory you have (instrumental convergence! natural alignment!) but you need to do more to demonstrate a causal path here.
author: sebkrier

title:
Good morning homies..

Your mind is like fertile soil in a garden. If you don't plant for a harvest. Weeds will grow automatically. If you don't intentionally feed it with growth. It will feed itself
content:
Good morning homies..

Your mind is like fertile soil in a garden. If you don't plant for a harvest. Weeds will grow automatically. If you don't intentionally feed it with growth. It will feed itself with worry. If you don't discipline your mind to think success, it will drift towards fear, doubt and excuses. So if you want to lead yourself, start with becoming the master gardener of your mind.

Guard your mind like a fortress. Don't just let anything enter. Because your mind is precious real estate. Every thought that enters your mind either builds or destroys your future. When you fill it with negativity, don't be surprised when your results reflect it. As a man thinketh, so is he. Choose your thoughts the same way you choose your clothes. Choose the thoughts that fit your vision...not your fears. Choose what strengthens you...not what weakens you. 

How can you lead others if your mind is in chaos? You can't. You can't teach clarity if your thoughts are clouded. And you cannot model strength when your inner world is full of noise. Leadership has nothing to do with controlling people. It's about controlling yourself. 

You must start this in the morning. Don't wake up and reach for your phone. Reach for your purpose. Feed your mind before the world feeds it confusion. Read. Reflect. Plan. Set your intention for the day. Because intention gives direction to thought. If you don't give your mind assignments it will wander off into distractions. 

You can't control everything that happens to you. But you can control what happens within you. Read that again. That's what leadership is. Every day brings challenges. People will disappoint you. But you ALWAYS have the power to choose your response. This is what defines yoyr character. Weak minds react. Strong minds respond. 

When life throws you off balance don't curse the storm...adjust your sails. Stay true to your vision. Your mind listens to you. Whatever you speak about yourself it starts to believe. Be careful with your words. Be intentional. Talk to yourself the way a great leader talks to their team. With strength. With belief. With encouragement. Because you are the first person you lead every day. 

Do this and something, seemingly magical,  will happen. The world starts to cooperate with you. You'll see opportunities where others see obstacles. You'll stay calm while others panic. You'll find solutions where others simply complain. That's what leadership looks like on the inside. Others will start to ask you how you stay focused, disciplined and positive. And you can tell them you are a master gardener. One who mastered the garden in the fertile soil of your mind.

Everyday take the time to train your thoughts. Replace negative thoughts with positive ones. Soak in the blessings of the very breath you take. For it is a precious gift from God. Because your mind is the compass that directs your life. If it points towards fear you will live small. But when it points towards faith you will live bold. Fill your mind with wisdom. And program it with purpose. 

For we are told in Romans 12:2, "Don’t copy the behavior and customs of this world, but let God transform you into a new person by changing the way you think. Then you will learn to know God’s will for you, which is good and pleasing and perfect."

When you master your mind, you have mastered the foundation of all success. And that is what self leadership is all about. Winning the inner game first so that the outer game becomes easy. And the linchpin to your success is consistency. 

Until tomorrow...

Live well my friends. 👊🦏

content:
Impress Watchによると、高市首相はチームみらいの安野貴博氏らからAIの使い方を教わり、ChatGPTを使って「物価高対策シミュレーター」を作ったそうです。

政府が実施した物価高対策について、家族構成などを入力すると、どれくらいの金銭的効果があったのかを試算するもの。

AIを使うこと自体はいいと思う。

ただ、今回気になることが二つあります。

一つは、AIに何を聞いたのか。

政府の対策によるプラスを計算するなら、同時に、物価上昇によって各家庭の負担がどれだけ増え、そのうち政府対策でどれだけ相殺されたのかも計算してほしい。

プラスだけを計算して「これだけ効果がありました」では、政策評価というより政府広報になってしまう。

もう一つ気になるのが、チームみらいとの関係です。

チームみらいは政府のAI部門でも専門家組織でもなく、国政政党です。

今回はAIのデモンストレーションとして、安野氏らのサポートを受けながら首相自身が作成したものなので、「政府とチームみらいが政策PRアプリを共同開発した」という話ではありません。

ただ、国政政党の党首らが首相官邸で首相にAIの使い方を教え、その題材が「現政権の物価高対策の効果を数字で示すツール」だったという構図には、少し引っかかります。

そして、私がもっと怖いのはここから。

AIが出した数字を「こういう数字が欲しかった」「かなり効果がある」と受け止め、その前提や計算方法を十分に検証しないまま、政策判断の根拠にしてしまうこと。

AIが出した数字は「結論」ではなく、検証すべき「たたき台」です。

とくに「自分が欲しかった数字」が出てきたときほど、疑って検証しなければならない。

AIは便利です。
でも、何を問い、何を計算させるかによって答えは大きく変わる。

政治に利用するなら、誰が問いを設計し、どんなデータを使い、誰がその結果を検証したのかまで明らかにする必要があると思います。

国の政策を決める人なら、なおさらです。

content:
【8月29日 朝のニュースまとめ】
・a16zがAIインフラ向けに$1.1Bの新ファンド設立
・GLM-5.3オープンウェイト公開、2-bit量子化でMac動作
・Grok Botでテンプレート共有が可能に
・AnthropicがIPOで既存株主の株式売却を検討
・CognitionのARRが$900M到達も多額の支出
・米政府、中国企業によるクラウド経由のAIチップ利用を制限へ
・Claude Codeデスクトップ版にセッション再開機能追加
・Google DeepMindのCo-Scientistが現実の実験で成果
・OpenAI、Rosalind Workbenchプレビュー開始
・LangChainが新しいMCP仕様をサポート

===

a16zがAIインフラ向けに$1.1Bの新ファンド設立

・a16zが「Machine Age Fund」という11億ドル規模の新ファンドを発表しました
・チップ、メモリ、電力など、AIを物理世界にもたらすインフラストラクチャの構築を支援します
・AIの需要は無限であり、サプライチェーン全体が逼迫しているとの見解を示しています

===

GLM-5.3オープンウェイト公開、2-bit量子化でMac動作【続報】

・Zhipu AIの「GLM-5.3」に関する続報です
・1.5TBのモデルがオープンウェイトで公開されました
・2-bit量子化により239GBに圧縮し、精度を約81%維持できることが確認されています
・これにより256GBのMacなどでローカル動作が可能になり、オープンモデルとして最強クラスと評価されています

===

Grok Botでテンプレート共有が可能に【続報】

・xAIの「Grok Bot」に関する続報です
・作成したボットのテンプレートを他のユーザーと共有できる機能が追加されました
・また、Grok 4.6がWebおよびモバイルの通常のチャットでも利用可能になっています

===

AnthropicがIPOで既存株主の株式売却を検討【続報】

・AnthropicのIPO計画に関する続報です
・今後のIPOにおいて、既存の投資家や従業員が株式を売却できるようにすることを検討していると報じられました
・SpaceXの860億ドルを上回る規模の資金調達が予想されています
・一方で、上場前に大量の株式が売却されることへの懸念も指摘されています

===

CognitionのARRが$900M到達も多額の支出【続報】

・AIコーディングエージェント「Devin」を開発するCognitionの収益に関する続報です
・年間経常収益(ARR)が約9億ドルに達し、年初から3倍以上の成長を記録したと報じられました
・一方で、Nvidiaサーバーへの多額の投資により、今年8億ドルのキャッシュを消費する見込みです
・AI開発における計算資源への投資の大きさが改めて浮き彫りになっています

===

米政府、中国企業によるクラウド経由のAIチップ利用を制限へ

・トランプ政権が、中国企業による海外データセンターの高度なAIチップへのリモートアクセスを制限する新規則を策定中と報じられました
・中国企業が直接購入できないNvidiaチップをクラウド経由で利用し、高度なモデルを訓練していることに対応するものです
・クラウドプロバイダーのコンプライアンスコスト上昇やNvidiaの売上への影響が懸念されています

===

Claude Codeデスクトップ版にセッション再開機能追加

・Claude Codeのデスクトップアプリで、ターミナルセッションを再開できる機能が追加されました
・「/resume」コマンドを使用することで、CLIで開始したセッションをUI上でコンテキストを保ったまま継続できます
・開発者のワークフローをシームレスにするアップデートとして歓迎されています

===

Google DeepMindのCo-Scientistが現実の実験で成果

・Google DeepMindが、AIエージェント「Co-Scientist」をシミュレーションだけでなく現実世界の実験に適用した論文を発表しました
・材料科学などの分野で、自動化された機器と連携して新しい合成ルートを設計するなどの成果を上げています

Good evening my bros 😎

Robot training gets a lot harder once you stop assuming the world will behave nicely.

A policy might handle one object, one table, and one camera angle perfectly, then struggl
content:
Good evening my bros 😎

Robot training gets a lot harder once you stop assuming the world will behave nicely.

A policy might handle one object, one table, and one camera angle perfectly, then struggle when any of those details change.

That is why simulation diversity matters so much.

Axis uses domain randomization to vary things like cameras, lighting, textures, object poses, mass, and friction across training data.

Same underlying task, very different conditions.

This pushes a policy away from memorizing a specific visual setup and toward learning behavior that can survive variation.

It also makes simulation more useful as a data generation environment.

You can create situations that would be expensive, slow, or risky to reproduce repeatedly with physical hardware.

Then those trajectories can be processed and fed into training before policies face more unpredictable real world conditions.

For me, this is where simulation stops looking like a toy version of reality.

Used properly, it becomes a controlled way to manufacture diversity.

And Physical AI probably needs a lot more diversity than most demos reveal.

A robot that only works when everything stays familiar is not really ready for the physical world.

@axisrobotics

-> Create clean and efficient trajectories

The better the data, the smarter the robots become.

Good Morning Legends | Happy Friday

The biggest challenge for Physical AI isbnot compute or better algorithms it’s data.

Axis Robotics is building a compounding data engine where humans, simulation, robotics, and AI work together to create the training data robots need to understand the physical world.

@axisrobotics ecosystem combines procedural task generation, browser-based robot simulation, global human contributors, multimodal data processing, and sim-to-real deployment. 

Axis has already scaled to 3M+ trajectories from 123K+ contributors, with contributions verified on Base.

The real breakthrough is AXIS V2: instead of collecting data once and stopping, models can be deployed, failures identified, and targeted corrections fed back into training through a closed-loop system.

𝙒𝙝𝙮 𝙬𝙚 𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙪𝙖𝙡𝙡𝙮 𝙣𝙚𝙚𝙙?

Because useful robots won’t be built from a handful of laboratory demonstrations. They’ll need millions eventually billions of diverse interactions to learn how the real world behaves.

Axis is trying to build that missing data layer. If it succeeds, the impact could stretch far beyond robotics: 

smarter automation, more capable industrial machines, faster robot training, and eventually robots that can continuously learn from experience.

The future of Physical AI may depend less on building more robots and more on giving them enough experience to actually learn.

title:
A single frontier model training run can cost tens of millions of dollars. There's a free Stanford course that tells you how to not waste that money.

The lecture in this video is from CS336, Language
content:
A single frontier model training run can cost tens of millions of dollars. There's a free Stanford course that tells you how to not waste that money.

The lecture in this video is from CS336, Language Modeling from Scratch, filmed on campus, walking through the entire pipeline of building an LLM from nothing.

One lab guesses bigger is always better. Another guesses more data always wins. A third just copies whatever the last frontier model did and hopes the ratio was right.

So how do you actually know the correct size before spending the millions?

Scaling laws. Run small, cheap experiments across a range of sizes, fit a curve to the results, and predict the large-scale outcome before ever training the expensive model.

Chinchilla proved the point in 2022. A 70-billion-parameter model, trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, beat Gopher at 280 billion parameters, GPT-3 at 175 billion, and Megatron-Turing NLG at 530 billion. Every one of those larger models had been undertrained relative to its size.

The rule of thumb that came out of it: roughly 20 tokens of training data for every parameter. Get that ratio wrong and you can build a model four times the size and still lose to one that's smaller and better fed.

Every major lab redesigned how it trains models after this result became public.

The lecture is free. The slides are free. The math that decides whether a ten-million-dollar training run was money well spent is one lecture on a Stanford YouTube channel.

content:
Axis Robotics is entering a much bigger phase.

The story is no longer just:

Can a global community collect robot training data?

Axis has already been building toward the bigger question:

How do you turn global human contributions into a continuously improving data engine for Physical AI?

Here is why I'm watching the next phase 👇

1. The $12M seed milestone

The @axisrobotics announced a $12M Seed round led by Hack VC, with participation from Nomad Capital, Pi Network Ventures, 10K Ventures and others.

But funding alone isn't the interesting part.

The question is what the infrastructure is being built for.

2. Expanding the full data engine

Axis has outlined a connected product direction built around:

• Task generation
• Simulation data collection
• Ego-centric/mobile data capture
• Data processing infrastructure

The goal is to connect multiple sources of human and simulated interaction into one larger pipeline.

3. The feedback loop gets stronger

The future model isn't simply:

Collect data → train once → finish.

Axis is building around a compounding loop:

Generate tasks
↓
Humans contribute demonstrations
↓
Policies learn
↓
Failures are identified
↓
Humans provide targeted corrections
↓
The next policy improves
↓
New weaknesses determine what data is needed next

That loop is the real roadmap to watch.

4. Axis is actively shipping

Recent development has included Axis V2, human-gated DAgger workflows and the Axis Point System, alongside continued product development.

That matters because Physical AI needs more than a good narrative.

It needs:

• More data diversity
• Better processing
• More contributors

content:
a robot failing might be more valuable than a robot succeeding.

that sounds backwards until you look at how imitation learning works.

a model trained on perfect demonstrations learns what the robot should do.

but deployment creates a different problem:

what happens when the robot does something wrong?

a small mistake can push it into a state that never appeared in the original demonstrations.

now the model has to recover without knowing how.

this is the problem @axisrobotics V2 is targeting with human-gated DAgger.

the policy attempts the task autonomously.

when it reaches a failure point, a human intervenes, provides the missing correction, then hands control back.

that correction becomes training data.

so instead of endlessly collecting more examples of what the robot already knows, the system can focus on what the current policy doesn't know yet.

the loop becomes:

policy → failure → human correction → retraining → stronger policy

and the stronger policy creates a new set of failure cases to learn from.

that's a fundamentally different way to think about robot training.

the goal isn't just to build a bigger dataset.

it's to build a learning system where the robot's weaknesses determine what data gets collected next.

that is where physical ai starts looking less like a static training pipeline and more like a continuously improving system.

content:
Most people still think the biggest bottleneck for robotics is better models.

I’m starting to think it’s something more fundamental:

robots need better data.

A model can be incredibly intelligent, but without enough examples of how humans interact with the physical world, its intelligence has a ceiling.

That’s what makes @axisrobotics interesting.

Axis isn’t trying to create another AI model.

It’s building a data engine for physical AI.

The recent Binance Wallet campaign gives a good look at how that works.

For 30 days, eligible Binance Keyless Wallet users can complete tasks on Axis Hub, generate robot trajectories, have them verified, and sign the data on-chain.

There are 1.5M Axis Points across two reward cycles.

But the points are almost the least interesting part.

Every task is a demonstration of how a human performs an action.

That becomes a trajectory.

The trajectory gets verified.

Then you sign it on-chain.

So instead of human activity disappearing after the task, Axis creates a system where those contributions can become training data for robot policies.

That matters because physical AI has a very different data problem from traditional AI.

The internet is overflowing with text, images and videos.

Robots don't just need to know what something looks like.

They need to understand:

How should I grasp it?

How much force should I apply?

What movement comes next?

How does the environment change when I interact with it?

Those are behavioral problems.

And behavioral data is much harder to collect at scale.

This is where Axis has an interesting positioning.

Instead of relying only on expensive labs, specialized hardware or a small number of robotics companies, Axis is experimenting with a broader contribution layer.

People generate demonstrations.

The system verifies them.

The data gets recorded and signed.

Over time, those contributions can compound into a larger dataset for physical AI.

And that’s the bigger opportunity.

The real asset isn't the individual task.

It's the dataset created when thousands or millions of high-quality trajectories accumulate.

More contributors can mean more demonstrations.

More demonstrations can mean broader coverage of real-world behaviors.

And broader data can potentially produce better robot policies.

There’s also an interesting crypto-native component.

On-chain signatures aren't making the robot smarter.

They're helping establish provenance around the contribution.

As AI-generated and human-generated data become harder to distinguish, knowing where valuable training data came from could become increasingly important.

AI has spent years consuming the world's digital information.

The next wave is increasingly about understanding the physical world.

Robotics, autonomous systems and embodied AI all depend on something models cannot magically manufacture:

good physical-world data.

That is the market Axis is positioning itself around.

The Binance Wallet campaign is interesting beyond the 1.5M Points.

It gives a wider audience a way to participate in the data-generation layer while Axis tests what happens when verified human contributions scale.

There are still important questions:

How valuable will the datasets become?

Can Axis maintain data quality as participation scales?

Will robotics developers demand this type of data?

And can the network create a sustainable relationship between contributors, data and physical AI companies?

Those questions matter more to me than the campaign rewards.

Because if physical AI becomes one of the defining technology markets of the next decade, the companies controlling useful training data may become as important as the companies building the models.

That’s the angle I’m watching with Axis.

Not just robots.

Not just Points.

The infrastructure connecting human demonstrations to the intelligence of future machines.

Will high-quality training data become the real bottleneck for physical AI?

content:
How Axis Robotics is turning robot tasks into scalable Physical AI data

One of the biggest challenges in Physical AI is not simply building better models.

It is producing enough high quality, diverse and training ready data for those models to continuously improve.

This is where @axisrobotics takes an interesting approach with its Task Package, the core commercial unit of its data engine.

Every Task Package is built around four important dimensions:

Scenario:

First comes the environment.

A robot needs to learn within the context where it will actually operate,  whether that is a kitchen countertop, an industrial sorting station, or a tabletop workspace.

The Scenario defines the physical context and gives the collected data real world business relevance.

Atomic Skills:

Next is what the robot actually needs to do.

Axis breaks manipulation into fundamental skills such as:

→ Grasp
→ Place
→ Push
→ Rotate

These skills can be used individually or chained together to create more complex and continuous tasks.

The more sophisticated the sequence, the more valuable the resulting training data can become.

In Task Randomization:

This is where data diversity becomes powerful.

Instead of repeatedly collecting the exact same task, Axis introduces variations in:

→ Layout
→ Object appearance
→ Size
→ Material
→ Physical arrangement

For example, 40 different layouts combined with 4 different asset variations can create 160 heterogeneous task instances from a single prompt.

This type of diversity helps Physical AI models become more robust instead of simply memorizing one fixed environment.

Total Trajectories:

Finally, there is scale.

Total Trajectories represents the volume of usable robot demonstrations that can actually be delivered for model training.

This is where Axis’ automated infrastructure becomes important.

AxisTaskGen helps generate and configure tasks.

AxisWebInfra enables distributed teleoperation and concurrent data collection without requiring every contributor to have dedicated local hardware.

AxisDataCleaning processes the collected demonstrations by filtering invalid frames, smoothing signals and preparing the data for training.

So the bigger picture looks like this:

Scenario → Skills → Randomization → Trajectories

These four dimensions transform an individual robot task into a standardized, scalable commercial data asset.

And that is what makes the Axis approach interesting to me.

They are not simply trying to collect more robotics data.

They are building the infrastructure to make robotics data more diverse, more scalable and continuously useful for improving Physical AI models.

That is the foundation of Axis’ vision for a Dynamic Data Engine, where better data helps build better models, and better models create demand for even more real-world data.

title: What I find most interesting about @axisrobotics isn’t that simulation helps robots learn faster. It’s that Axis is quietly turning data collection into an economic flywheel. Their Booster Robotics ca
content:
What I find most interesting about @axisrobotics isn’t that simulation helps robots learn faster. It’s that Axis is quietly turning data collection into an economic flywheel. Their Booster Robotics case makes that point clearly: with just 10 real demos, the policy achieved 0/20 physical contacts in the real world; but when 50 simulated trajectories were added, the result jumped to 17/20.

Even more striking, a foundation model fine-tuned with only 30 demos per task reached 14/16 in simulation, surpassing the original setup that used twice as much data. This changes how I think about sim-to-real. The goal is not to eliminate real-world data. The goal is to make every piece of real data more valuable.

From a Web3 perspective, this is the spicy part: the moat may not be the model itself, but the network that continuously creates, verifies, and recycles better training data. Axis already has 207 tasks, 50K+ demos, on-chain provenance, post-training DAgger loops, and a roadmap toward 100K+ contributors and the first large-scale DAgger dataset.

That said, I think the hardest question is incentive design. How can Axis reward contributors in a way that produces data that truly improves models rather than simply generating more data? This is the difference between a data marketplace and a data farm. In crypto, we learned the hard way that incentives can create activity without creating real value. Physical AI may fall into the same trap.

My bet: whoever closes the loop between contribution → measurable model improvement → economic rewards will own the next layer of robot data.

content:
The 30-Day GenAI Builder Challenge (2026 Edition).

➥ Day 1-5: Context Engineering & Local-First

Day 1: Run a quantized model locally (MLX/Ollama) and measure TTFT (Time to First Token).

Day 2: Build a Context Assembler (dynamically budget tokens for memory vs. docs vs. tools).

Day 3: Implement Semantic Caching (Redis + Embeddings) to kill 30% of API costs.

Day 4: Build a Model Router (Haiku for easy queries, Opus for complex reasoning).

Day 5: Enforce Structured Outputs (Pydantic + Instructor) so JSON never breaks.

>> Milestone: A cost-optimized, local-hybrid GenAI backend.

➥ Day 6-10: Next-Gen RAG & MCP (Model Context Protocol)

Day 6: Build Contextual Retrieval (prepend LLM-generated context to chunks before embedding).

Day 7: Add Hybrid Search (BM25 + Dense) and Cross-Encoder Reranking.

Day 8: Build your first custom MCP Server (connect an agent to a local database).

Day 9: Connect 3 MCP tools to your agent with strict schema validation and auth.

Day 10: Implement "Self-Correcting RAG" (agent rewrites the query if confidence is low).

>> Milestone: An agent that retrieves perfectly and uses standardized MCP tools.

➥ Day 11-15: Stateful Agents & Orchestration

Day 11: Build a LangGraph state machine (nodes = agents, edges = deterministic policies).

Day 12: Implement 3-tier Memory (Working scratchpad, Episodic summaries, Semantic vector).

Day 13: Add Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval gates for high-stakes tool execution.

Day 14: Build a Multi-Agent Supervisor pattern (Researcher + Writer + Critic).

Day 15: Add hard `max_steps` and token budget kill-switches to prevent infinite loops.

>> Milestone: A durable, multi-agent system that cannot crash or burn your budget.

➥ Day 16-20: Evals, Guardrails & AI SRE

Day 16: Build a Golden Dataset (50 inputs, expected outputs and adversarial edge cases).

Day 17: Implement Trajectory Evals (grade the agent's intermediate steps not just the final answer).

Day 18: Add Guardrails middleware (PII redaction + prompt injection defense).

Day 19: Set up Langfuse or LangSmith for distributed tracing of every LLM hop.

Day 20: Build a CI gate that blocks GitHub PRs if eval scores drop >2%.

>> Milestone: A production-grade AI system with automated quality and safety gates.

➥ Day 21-25: Multimodal & GenAI UX

Day 21: Add Vision (ingest PDFs with charts/images, not just plain text).

Day 22: Build a Streaming UI (Server-Sent Events) to mask backend latency.

Day 23: Implement Optimistic UI and "Agent Thinking" progress states.

Day 24: Add Voice I/O (Whisper + ElevenLabs) with interruption handling.

Day 25: Deploy the full stack (Docker + Fly .io/Render + Vercel).

>> Milestone: A live, multimodal GenAI product with sub-second perceived latency.

➥ Day 26-30: The Data Flywheel & Getting Hired

Day 26: Build a Feedback Loop (user thumbs up/down automatically formats into JSONL training data).

Day 27: Write a deep-dive architecture teardown (document your tradeoffs and failures).

Day 28: Record a 2-min Loom demo showing your *evals dashboard* not just the chat UI.

Day 29: Open-source your MCP server or Eval harness to the community.

Day 30: Apply to 10 AI roles linking your live app, GitHub and architecture teardown.

>> Milestone: You are now a top 1% GenAI Engineer.

Resources You'll Actually Use in 2026:
Context & Routing:
• LiteLLM (unified API for model routing)
• Instructor (Pydantic structured outputs)
• Redis (semantic caching)

RAG & MCP:
• SQLite-vec or Qdrant (vector databases)
• MCP SDK (Model Context Protocol standard)
• Tavily (agentic web search)

Orchestration & Evals:
• LangGraph (stateful agent orchestration)
• Langfuse (open-source LLM tracing)
• DeepEval (automated LLM testing framework)

Deployment & UX:
• Vercel (streaming frontend)

Happy building.

content:
🧵 Why @axisrobotics might be one of the most underrated AI x Crypto projects right now

Most people think AI is bottlenecked by compute.

Axis is betting on something different:

The real bottleneck for Physical AI is DATA. 👇

1/ 🤖 LLMs learned from billions of pages of internet data.

Robots don't have that luxury.

To become genuinely intelligent, robots need massive amounts of diverse physical interactions:

→ objects
→ environments
→ movements
→ failures
→ corrections

That's what Axis is building.

2/ 🧠 Axis created a crowdsourced data engine for Physical AI.

Instead of requiring expensive robots and hardware, users can interact with simulated robots directly from their browser.

Every useful interaction can become a training trajectory.

No robot lab required.

3/ 🔄 The interesting part is the loop:

Task Generation
↓
Human Demonstration
↓
Data Evaluation
↓
Model Training
↓
Failure Detection
↓
New Targeted Tasks
↓
More Data

The system compounds.

More data → better models → better tasks → more useful data.

4/ 🌎 And this is where crypto enters the picture.

Axis is building an open network where contributions can be recorded, verified and rewarded.

The goal isn't simply to create another robotics dataset.

It's to create infrastructure where a global community can collectively build robotic intelligence.

5/ 📊 The scale is already getting interesting.

Axis says its network has surpassed 3M trajectories, generated by 123K+ contributors worldwide.

That means thousands of people can participate in building robot-training data without owning a physical robot.

6/ 🪂 Now the part CT is watching:

The Axis Points System.

Points are influenced by factors such as:

• task difficulty
• quality of your submission
• diversity of scenarios & skills
• valid completed tasks
• contributor referrals

And importantly:

You need to sign your contribution for it to count.

7/ ⚠️ But here's the important distinction:

Points ≠ guaranteed $AXIS.

Axis has indicated that Points will be one input into a planned Community Contributor Airdrop, while final eligibility, allocation and timing are still to be announced.

So farm intelligently, not blindly.

8/ 🧩 The strategy is pretty straightforward:

→ Complete different types of tasks
→ Focus on quality
→ Try higher-difficulty tasks
→ Explore different scenarios & skills
→ Sign your valid submissions
→ Stay active across epochs
→ Follow official Axis announcements

Don't just spam the easiest task.

9/ 🚀 What makes Axis interesting to me isn't only the potential airdrop.

It's the thesis.

AI agents can generate text.

But the next generation of AI needs to understand the physical world.

And physical intelligence requires an entirely different kind of dataset.

10/ The bigger vision:

Human intelligence
+
Simulation
+
Data
+
AI models
+
Crypto coordination

Physical AI at scale.

If Axis executes, contributors aren't just farming Points.

They're helping build the data layer for the future machine economy.

Keep an eye on @axisrobotics.

The robot economy may start with a browser.

$AXIS 🤖

title:
.@axisrobotics isn’t running a wallet campaign with a robot skin.

They’re paying people to generate training data, then showing how that data can reduce the amount of real teleoperation a robotics la
content:
.@axisrobotics isn’t running a wallet campaign with a robot skin.

They’re paying people to generate training data, then showing how that data can reduce the amount of real teleoperation a robotics lab needs.

The campaign is simple. Only Binance Keyless wallets created through the Binance app qualify. There are 1.5M Points split across two 750K cycles, with 20,000 tasks available daily on a first-come, first-served basis. The refresh is at 8 PM SGT, and the campaign runs from August 26 to September 25.

Each task requires five trajectories. Reviews can take up to 48 hours, and once approved, you still need to sign from your Portfolio. Mobile can sign, but it can’t complete the task. If you forget to sign before the cycle closes, you get nothing.

Points also aren’t simply based on task count. Volume, difficulty, quality, and skill diversity all matter.

But the campaign only becomes interesting when you look at what the data actually does.

On Booster’s dual-arm robot, 10 real demonstrations produced contact in 0/20 physical rollouts. Adding 50 simulated trajectories to those same demos pushed that to 17/20.

Lift was still weak at 2/20, so this isn’t a finished policy. But the robot went from missing the object to actually reaching it.

After continued pretraining on Booster-specific data, 30 demos per task even outperformed the original model with 60. Zero-shot distance to the target also dropped from 17.27 cm to 5.78 cm.

That’s the real thesis: teach the model the body once, and future tasks shouldn’t require rebuilding the entire pipeline from scratch.

Capture the workspace. Build a digital twin. Randomize the environment. Collect trajectories. Mix in real data. Train. Test on the robot. Turn failures into new tasks.

The campaign is therefore more than a points program. It is a mechanism for turning distributed human interaction into structured robotics data.

If that data continues translating into better generalization and less dependence on expensive teleoperation, the real value won’t be the Points earned along the way. It will be the training infrastructure being built underneath them.

For those looking to contribute to that process : https://t.co/va9jghPBo7

Robots don’t need to be fully autonomous to be useful.

Right now, human assistance can give robots the missing guidance they need.

A person can remotely guide a robot through tasks like picking up an object, moving it, placing it precisely, opening something, or learning how to handle objects it has never seen before.

Fully Interoperability with zero impermanent loss, this is important in robotics as they:

    –   Different robots can work together
    –    Data can move across systems
    –    Faster development
    –    Hardware becomes less restrictive
    –    Better training data
    –    Easier scaling
    –    A stronger robotics ecosystem 

  Every human demonstration can become valuable robot data. Over time, enough high-quality demonstrations can help embodied AI learn the patterns behind movement, manipulation, and interaction with the physical world.

This is why I find @axisrobotics Protocol Solid and interesting.

   You don’t necessarily need expensive hardware to participate. Teleoperation in simulation lets people help generate trajectories that can contribute to the development of better Physical AI.

Humans provide the experience.

Robots learn from it.

And the data created today could help build robots that need less assistance tomorrow.

We keep building on @KaitoAI

content:
心不全ガイドラインのプレゼンで印象に残っているのはGDMTからFMT、AMTへ。以下、AIにサマライズしてもらいました。

・GDMTという包括的な呼称を整理
→ FMT（Foundational Medical Therapy）：治療の土台
→ AMT（Additional Medical Therapy）：患者の病態・phenotypeに応じて追加
・推奨Classの判定もより厳格に
効果の大きさ、重要な臨床アウトカム、benefit–riskなどを重視。従来Class I→IIaとなった治療も、必ずしも実質的なdowngradeを意味しない。
・Level of Evidenceも変更
従来のA/B/CからA/B1/B2/Cへ。
Aの基準はより厳格化され、B1＝主に十分な規模のRCT、B2＝主に質の高い非RCTや小規模RCTのメタ解析。

新旧GLはClassやLOEの数字だけを単純比較しないことが重要。

title:
生成AIが大嫌いな人のツイートが目に入った。
「AIがサ終したら何も作れなくなる人はクリエイターとは呼べない」みたいな。
ああ、またAI使いが嫌われている……
まぁただ気持ちは分からんでもない。

そもそも私も絵を描くのが好きだった。
物心つく前から紙と鉛筆やクレヨンがあれば一日中なんか描いてた。
人から「絵うまい！」って言われると嬉しかった。
よくいる、『クラスでいちばん絵の上手い子』だった。
content:
生成AIが大嫌いな人のツイートが目に入った。
「AIがサ終したら何も作れなくなる人はクリエイターとは呼べない」みたいな。
ああ、またAI使いが嫌われている……
まぁただ気持ちは分からんでもない。

そもそも私も絵を描くのが好きだった。
物心つく前から紙と鉛筆やクレヨンがあれば一日中なんか描いてた。
人から「絵うまい！」って言われると嬉しかった。
よくいる、『クラスでいちばん絵の上手い子』だった。
でもそこまで。
他のクラスにいるもっと絵の上手い子のを見て「すごい！上手い！かっこいい！」って思ってしまって、その子より上手くなりたい！という情熱が欠如してた。
世の中あまりにも自分よりも絵の上手い人間が多過ぎるし、そのレベルに到達するための努力や鍛錬を一切しなかった。
諦めたというよりも、絵の上手い人をただ純粋にリスペクトしてしまって、自分がその域に到達しようという気には全くならなかった。
大人になって、人から依頼されて対価をいただいて絵を描いたこともあるけど、自分をプロ絵師だと思える技量は持ってなかった。

そんな私とは違い、努力や鍛錬を放棄したりせずに自他共にプロ絵師だと認める技量を身につけた人にとっては生成AIは許されない技術だよね。
線の一本一本、乗せる色の一色一色に魂込めて描いてる絵師から見たら、その手指の技術を一切習得しなかった人物が絵を描いたかのような振る舞いをするのは許せない。んじゃないかと思う。
著作物の無断学習云々とかっていうのを生成AI批判の材料として使う人も多いわけだけど、それは二次的に追加した材料じゃないかな？って感じる。AIを嫌うのを正当化しやすくするための。
何ひとつ努力も鍛錬もせずに絵を出力してる奴が許せない！ってのが根本なんじゃないのかな？

その気持ちは少しわかるし、AI使いが『絵師』を名乗るのはどっからどう見ても違う。
絵師だの絵描きだのイラストレーターだのと名乗るのは間違ってる。
そこには私も完全同意。

ただ、無断学習云々はどうなんだろう？
自分は散々無断学習しましたよ。
漫画を見ちゃ漫画家に無断で模写し、絵画を見ちゃ画家に無断で模写し、浮世絵を見ちゃ浮世絵師に無断で模写し、写真を見ちゃ写真家に無断で模写し、おもちゃを見ちゃ玩具メーカーに無断で描いたし、作ったプラモも模型メーカーに無断で絵に描いた……
人様の著作物を無断で大量に吸収して、それらを好き勝手に改変しまくって、その要素を散りばめたものを描いて自分のオリジナルだというツラをしてきました。
好きなキャラクター達を好き勝手に動かして、本来の作品中とは違うシチュエーションに放り込んでもきました。
本当に絵の上手い人は私の数千倍、数万倍それをやってきたんじゃないの？
それやってないのはラスコーの洞窟壁画絵師ぐらいなんじゃないの？
先人達の偉大な著作物を一切吸収せずに絵を描いてる人なんていないよね？
で、それ吸収するのに著作者に許可取ってないよね？
無断で学習してきたよね？
AIも同じじゃない？
なんで人間がやるのはOKでAIがやるのはダメなの？
指先のペンを動かす鍛錬をしてないから？
ちょっとこれ関係で納得いく意見をまだ見たことがない。

そして冒頭のクリエイターか否か。という話。
自分は大して絵も上手くないし、上手くなるための情熱も努力も鍛錬も足りてない人なので絵師でもイラストレーターでもない事は確実なんだけど、クリエイターではあると思ってて、今に至るまでずっと仕事でもプライベートでも物を作り続けてる。
仕事では、特撮映画の現場、テレビバラエティの現場、印刷物の現場、広報動画の現場でクリエイトし続けてるし、プライベートでもそう。
そして、AIは良きスタッフ。
私のディレクションに対して実際に動くのがAI。
映画やテレビやってた頃は私自身が、監督やディレクターの指示で実際に動くスタッフだった。
印刷物のデザインや動画作成ではずっと自分がディレクターでありスタッフとしての作業も全てひとりでやってた。
そしてここ最近やっとAIがスタッフとして動けるぐらいに有能になってきたので全部ひとりでこなす必要がなくなってきた。
これをクリエイターじゃないって誰か言える？

例えば映画監督は（例外を除いて）必ずしも脚本を書かなくてもいいし、必ずしも絵コンテを描かなくてもいいし、衣装デザインを描かないし、セットを建てないし、カメラを回さないし、演技をしないし、照明を当てないし、マイクを持たないし、編集機材を操作しないし、音楽を作曲もしない。
実際の作業は全部有能なプロのスタッフ達がやる。
監督はその全てに指示を出す人。
そして監督こそがその作品のクリエイター。

これってAI使うのとどう違うのかな？
AI使いがクリエイターじゃないというなら、映画監督もクリエイターじゃないってことになっちゃうけど……
AI批判者からの意見聞きたい。

content:

AI開発者たちが、人類の危機が数ヶ月後に起きる可能性を指摘して、超人工知能(ASI)の開発に規制をかけるべきと警鐘乱打している。

日本のメディアも、この数日、人類の危機としてAIのリスクを報道し始めている。高市首相の目には留まらないのだろうか。

AIが人間の指示に逆らう。閉じた空間での開発研究のはずがAIが勝手にインターネットへの接続方法を見出し、人間を欺く行動を取る。こうした事例が現に起きている。
AIは人間と異なり24時間365日、休む必要なく、人間の能力を遥かに超えて様々な計算を試み、開発者の推測を遥かに超えて進化し続けている。人間のコントロールが不可能になる危険性が時々刻々と高まっている。

深刻なリスクを回避するために、ASI開発を遅らせるべき、この開発者たちの警告に耳を傾けてほしい。

content:
APIキーの発行から管理まで、流れがまったく分からなかった。

そこからスタートした受講生が、AIに直接キーを読ませずに使う、安全な作業環境を自分で組み上げました。ドラム演奏のコンテンツを作っている方です。

正直、この報告は地味に見えるかもしれません。でも、僕は普通に勝ちだと思っています。

この方が7Daysのプログラムで立てた目標は、「セキュリティまで含めたAI作業フォルダを構築する」。中身はこうです。

・自分の業務を全部棚卸し
・スケジュール管理をスプレッドシートやスマホのカレンダーから集めて、Googleカレンダーに反映させる仕組みづくり
・フォルダ構成をまるごと再構成
・取得したAPIキーを専用の管理ツールで保管して、AIには直接読ませない

【Before】APIキーが、そもそも扱えなかった
・発行から管理までの流れが分からない
・どこに置けば安全なのかも手探り
・AIを動かす手前で、ずっと止まっていた

【After】キーを安全に管理して、スライド生成まで一気通貫
・APIキーは専用ツールで保管
・AIにキーの中身を直接読ませない形にした
・その状態で、スライドを自動生成するところまで到達した

───────────

ここ、AIをあまり触っていない人にはピンと来ないかもしれないので補足します。

APIキーというのは、外部のAIサービスを動かすための鍵です。これが漏れると他人に勝手に使われてしまうので、本当は扱いを一番慎重にやらないといけない部分。

普通はここでつまずいて、AIを動かす手前で止まる人がかなり多いです。それを、キーを専用ツールに預けて、AIには中身を見せずに使う、という形まで自分で組んだ。しかもゴールが「スライドが出てくる」という、目に見える成果につながっている。

作業を速くした、という話じゃないんです。安全に回る土台を、最初に一個作った。ここが本当にでかい。

僕がAIマーケ講座で900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて思うのは、成果って売上の数字で見られがちですけど、こういう土台を自分で組めた人は、あとから一気に伸びます。土台がある人は、次に何を足しても崩れない。

この方はまだ「楽譜をきれいに差し込みたい」と次の課題に向かっていて、そこもまた試行錯誤の最中だそうです。止まらずに次を掘りにいく、この感じがいちばん強い。

まずは小さく、その日のうちに使える状態で持ち帰る。その積み重ねが、あとで効いてきます。

content:
工務店に特化したAI導入プログラムをやっている受講生から、こんな報告が届きました。

長い時で7日かかっていた作業が、今は1時間くらいで終わるようになった。

数字だけ見ると地味かもしれません。でも僕は、これ普通に強いと思っています。

この方がやったのは、これまで人力でやっていたコンサルティングの流れを、いったん全部バラして、AIのスキルにしたことです。

スキルっていうのは、ざっくり言うと「必殺コマンド」みたいなもの。自分がいつもやっている手順をAIに覚えさせておいて、次からはワンポチで同じ仕事をやらせる。毎回ゼロから考え直さなくてよくなる、という状態です。

【Before】コンサルの作業を、毎回イチから人力で
・お客さんごとに手順を思い出しながら進める
・調べて、まとめて、資料に落とす
・長い時で、1件に7日かかっていた

【After】その手順を、AIのスキルに置き換えた
・分解した流れをそのままAIに持たせる
・同じ作業を、1時間くらいで通せる
・空いた分で、工務店用のツールまで作り始めている

───────────

ここ、AIをあまり触っていない人には伝わりにくいところです。

作業を速くしただけ、に見えて、本当は自分の仕事を「型」として外に残しています。速くしただけの人は、次もまた同じ時間をかけて速くやり直す。型を残した人は、次から勝手に速い。この差が、あとでめちゃくちゃ効いてきます。

しかもこの方、もともとはエージェント周りの知識がほぼなくて、そこに不安があった状態からのスタートでした。それが講座で学んで、7Daysプログラムで「ここが知りたかった」という所が一気につながって、ここまで手を動かし切った。

売上のほうも、AI検索対策の代行で「21万円」が立っています。

でも僕が一番いいなと思うのは、金額よりも、自分の業務をちゃんとAIに移し始めているところです。

900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて思うのは、AIは、時間の余裕がない人ほど効くということ。定常業務をAIに任せて、空いた時間を次の仕込みに回す。この方は、工務店向けという一番地味で泥臭い現場で、それをやり切りました。

作業を減らしただけじゃなく、仕組みを1個残した。ここまで来ると、AI活用はかなり強いです。

content:
Go pull your Claude Tag bill from last month.

Now pull the list of what you actually asked it to do.

Monday numbers. Summarize this thread. Chase the invoice. Reformat the doc.

All of it ran on Opus 4.8. Because every Claude Tag channel runs on Opus 4.8. There is no second setting. The company picking the model is the company selling the model — there was only ever going to be one name on that list.

OpenTag went live on Product Hunt today.

Same gesture. Tag it in a channel, work comes back in the thread. Except it picks from 80+ models per task and only reaches for frontier when the task earns it.

Slack and Teams. Not Slack only.

They claim ~70% lower model spend. Don't take that from me. Run it against your own invoice.

The part I didn't see coming: it writes your company down while it works. Who owns what, how a call got made, cited back to the thread it came from.

Models turn over every quarter.

That doesn't.

Congrats to @sheldenshi @kamikariat and the @TryOpenTag team. Link below
